Daysman
DAYZ-man
noun
From the older English use of day for a day appointed for hearing a cause, hence a day’s-man — the man who sits on the appointed day: an umpire, an arbiter, a mediator empowered to judge between two parties and bind them both to his award.

Biblical Definition

A daysman is an umpire — the arbiter who sits on the day appointed to hear a cause, hears both parties, and lays his hand upon each to bind them to his judgment. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it is one of the deepest cries in the Old Testament. Job, crushed and misjudged, longs to bring his cause before God and knows he cannot: “For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment” (Job 9:32). The creature cannot summon the Creator to court; the gulf is infinite. So Job laments, “Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both” (Job 9:33). He wants an umpire who can touch God with one hand and man with the other — one who shares the nature of each, or he can lay hold of neither. No angel will serve, for an angel is not God; no prophet will serve, for a prophet is not God either. Job’s cry is answered in the fulness of time: “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Here is the daysman — true God of true God, and true man of the substance of His mother; one Person in two natures, united without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, as Chalcedon confessed. He lays one hand on God because He is God, and one hand on man because He is man, and He is not two mediators but one. “For this cause he is the mediator of the new testament” (Heb 9:15), and by His death the called receive the promise of eternal inheritance.

Webster 1828 Definition

An umpire or arbiter; one who sits on an appointed day to judge between two parties — in Job, the mediator man cannot find and God has given in Christ.

DAYSMAN, an umpire or arbiter; a mediator appointed to decide a cause.

From day, the day set for hearing, and man; the margin of Job reads “umpire.”

He lays his hand upon both parties, binding each to his award.

A KJV hapax: Job cries that no daysman stands betwixt him and God (Job 9:33).

The office is filled by the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus (1Ti 2:5).

Key Scripture

Job 9:33 — "Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both."

Job 9:32 — "For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment."

1Ti 2:5 — "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;"

Heb 9:15 — "And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance."

Modern Corruption

The umpire Job could not find and God has given. Two errors assault it: the religion of direct access without a mediator, and Rome’s intruding of many mediators against Scripture’s “one.”

expand to see more

The first corruption is the denial that any daysman is needed at all — the religion of direct access on one’s own terms, which walks into the presence of God as though no gulf were fixed and no wrath abode. Job knew better. He knew that God is not a man as he was, that they could not come together in judgment, and that without an umpire to lay a hand on both he had no standing and no hope. Every man who prays to a God he has never been reconciled to, who assumes a hearing he was never granted, is asking Job’s question and refusing Job’s answer. There is no coming to the Father but by the Son. To come without the daysman is to come without a hand to hold, and there is no other name given among men.

The second corruption runs the opposite way and is Rome’s: not too few mediators but too many. Scripture says one mediator between God and men, and Rome has interposed Mary as mediatrix, the saints as intercessors, and the priest at the altar — a whole scaffolding of daysmen erected against the plain word of 1Ti 2:5. The reason they cannot serve is the reason Chalcedon gives for why Christ can: the umpire must lay his hand upon both, and no creature, however honoured, can lay a hand on God. Mary was a sinner saved by her Son; the saints are debtors like ourselves; the priest has no blood of his own to bring. Only He who is one Person in two natures — without confusion, change, division, or separation — touches deity and humanity at once. Job asked for a daysman, and God gave him not a committee but a Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means an umpire or arbiter who sits on the appointed day and binds both parties to his judgment.

expand to see more

Daysman — from day (the day appointed to hear a cause) + man.

It denotes an umpire or arbiter; the Job margin reads “umpire.”

He lays his hand upon both parties, having authority over each.

Job found no daysman betwixt himself and God (Job 9:33).

Christ fills the office: God and man in one Person (1Ti 2:5).

Usage

"Job cried for a daysman to lay his hand upon both — and God answered with His Son."

"The daysman must touch both parties: only the God-man can reach heaven and earth at once."

"One mediator, not many: the office admits of no Mary, no saint, no priest beside Christ."
